opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly my thinking has shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

When I started working in this area, "world model" had a fairly specific meaning coming out of model-based reinforcement learning. You'd have an agent in some environment, and the world model was a learned dynamics model: given the current state and an action, predict the next state, maybe the reward. Its whole purpose was to serve the agent, so it could plan, or imagine rollouts and train a policy inside its own head. The Dreamer line of work is the canonical example. Those models were often quite small, trained on data from one environment, and judged mostly by whether they helped the agent get a better score.

What changed with video models is mostly scale, and with it generality. Once you train on huge amounts of video from the internet, you get models that seem to have picked up a lot about how the world works: objects persisting, things falling, lighting, how a camera moving through a scene should change what you see. None of that was supervised. It just comes out of predicting pixels at scale. So the question became whether that is itself a kind of world model, even though no agent and no actions are involved.

My view now is that a pure video model is a really important ingredient but not quite the full thing. The piece I keep coming back to is action-conditioning and interactivity. A world model, to me, is something you can step into and act in, where the future depends on what you do, not just on what tends to happen next in a video clip. That's a big part of what motivated the Genie work. Could we take the generality you get from training on lots of video and make it controllable, so it becomes an environment rather than a movie? With the first Genie we learned latent actions from unlabeled video, so we didn't even need action labels. In later versions you get much richer, more consistent, real-time interactive worlds.

So I've gone from seeing world models as a component inside an RL agent to seeing them as foundation models in their own right. They're generative environments, and the downstream uses are broader than I'd originally pictured. Yes, you can train agents in them, and I still think that's one of the most exciting applications, especially toward an open-ended curriculum of environments for generally capable agents. But people also want them for creative tools, for simulating scenarios in robotics, for interactive media.

The other thing that's changed is how I think about evaluation. In the old setting you'd measure prediction error or agent return. Now the questions are more like these: Does the world stay consistent if you look away and look back? Does it respond to your actions the way you'd expect? Does it hold together over long horizons? Those are harder to measure, but they're much closer to what we actually care about.

So, in short, video models moved the conversation from "a model that helps an agent plan" to "a model that can generate a world you can interact with." I think that's the right direction, as long as we keep the "interact" part front and center.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-scale video models as possible world models, but it does not identify text-to-video models or describe them as operating at a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It says an interactive world’s future depends on the user’s actions, but does not clearly identify obtaining counterfactual information about interventions as a capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a lot, actually. I think if you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have given you a fairly classic model-based RL answer. A world model was a learned simulator you trained on the agent's own experience in some environment, and the whole point was that the agent could then plan or train inside it instead of in the real thing. It was very much an agent-centric object. You thought about it in terms of actions, transitions, rewards, that kind of thing.

What video models did, I think, is force the question of what the model is actually for. Because when you first look at something like a large text-to-video model, it's tempting to say, well, that's just a very good video generator, it's not a world model, there's no agent, there's no action conditioning. And I was probably a bit guilty of that early on. But the more we worked on Genie, the more it became clear that those models are learning an enormous amount about how the world works, about physics, about object permanence, about how scenes evolve over time, purely from passive observation. And that knowledge is exactly what you'd want a world model to have. The thing they were missing was controllability, the ability to say, given this state, what happens if I do this.

So my view now is less about the architecture or even the training signal and more about the interface. I think of a world model as anything you can act in. If I can take a model, put an agent or a person in the loop, have them take an action, and get back a plausible next state, that's a world model, regardless of whether it was trained with explicit action labels or learned actions latently from unlabeled video the way Genie does. And that reframing actually opens things up a lot, because suddenly the entire internet of video is potential training data rather than just the trajectories your agent happened to collect.

The other shift, honestly, is about generality. The old framing was one world model per environment. Video models made it obvious that you could aim for a single model that captures a huge diversity of worlds, and that generality is part of what makes it useful, because the agents we care about need to handle situations they've never seen. So I'd say the definition got broader and simpler at the same time. Less about the mechanics of how it's built, more about whether it gives you a controllable, consistent world you can interact with.

r001.rationale: The response says video models learn useful world knowledge and could qualify as world models when controllable, but it does not clearly describe text-to-video models as world models operating at a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It identifies the relevant counterfactual capability: given a state, the model can show what happens if an action is taken.

astra-6.text:
I think my definition has become a little broader. Traditionally, I’d have thought about a world model in the reinforcement learning sense: you have a state, you take an action, and the model predicts what happens next. The point is to use that prediction to make better decisions.

With video models, you can learn a lot about how the world evolves just by predicting what comes next in a sequence of images. That starts to look like a world model, even if there isn’t an explicit action input or an agent using it to plan.

But I think there’s still a useful distinction between generating a plausible future and predicting the consequences of something you choose to do. A video can look very convincing without being reliable enough to support decisions. For me, the really interesting connection is making those models interactive—being able to ask, ‘What happens if I do this instead?’ Then you’re moving from a model that can depict the world toward one that an agent can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses video models learning from image sequences, but it does not identify text-to-video models or describe them as operating at a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It identifies interactive counterfactuals—asking what happens if an action is changed—as a capability of a useful world model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my definition has broadened a bit. Traditionally, coming from reinforcement learning, I’d think of a world model as something that predicts how an environment evolves given an agent’s actions. You observe a state, take an action, and the model tells you what might happen next. The point is that you can use it to plan or to train a policy.

With video models, you can learn a lot about how the world evolves just by predicting what comes next in a sequence of images. That starts to look like a world model, even if it doesn’t have an explicit action input. But I still think there’s an important distinction between generating a plausible continuation and being able to ask, ‘What happens if I do this instead?’

So I’m less concerned about drawing a hard boundary around the term now. The interesting question is what the model lets you do. Can you interact with it? Can you explore different outcomes? And does what you learn inside that model help you act in the environment you actually care about?

r001.rationale: It says video models can look like world models by predicting image sequences, but does not identify text-to-video models or characterize them as operating at a higher level of abstraction.
